title: Outsourced Political Campaign: Role of Pro-Government Political Influencers in Spreading Hostile Narratives in Hungary
screen_reason: Qualitative-only content analysis plus focus groups and an awareness survey; no quantitative share of content judged false or misleading, and no survey item asking about encountering misinformation. The 105 most-advertised Megafon videos were analysed qualitatively (narratives, linguistic and visual tools); the only counts given for them are topical (39/105 on Peter Magyar, 22/105 on the Ukraine war, 10/105 on the 'dollar left'), never a veracity coding, and the veracity claims are verbal ('most videos rely on demonization and fearmongering, often presenting distorted information'). The representative poll (n = 1,000) measures name recognition of the influencers (43%) and of the Megafon brand (20%), frequency of coming across Megafon clips among those already aware of them (34% at least weekly, n = 480), awareness that the clips are paid advertising (30%), and perceived credibility (64% say not credible) - i.e. brand awareness, encounter frequency and perception, not a share of respondents reporting exposure to false or misleading information. The one veracity share in the text (54% of political advertising featured hostile narratives) is attributed to Political Capital et al. (2024), a figure cited from elsewhere, which R8 forbids keeping. Grounds: qualitative-only for the content analysis; no share of items classified false; survey shares are not misinformation-exposure measures.
missed_or_uncertain:
ONE JUDGEMENT CALL AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD SEE. The nearest thing to an eligible estimate is: 'A third of the respondents (34%) who had heard of one of the influencers or the name Megafon came across videos associated with the group at least once a week' (Section 5.3; Figure 1 note gives the denominator as n = 480, respondents who knew at least one Megafon influencer or Megafon itself, out of a representative sample of 1,000 Hungarian adults polled 13-24 May 2024). This could be read as source-level self-reported exposure to a state-funded disinformation network, since the authors characterise Megafon as an organised disinformation operation. I did NOT extract it, for three reasons: (a) the survey item asks about encountering a named influencer group's video clips, not about false or misleading information, and no item of Megafon content is coded for veracity anywhere in the paper, so 'misinformation' is the authors' framing of the actor rather than a measured property of the content; (b) the denominator is conditional on prior awareness (n = 480 aware respondents, not the 1,000-person sample), and the authors explicitly say the poll 'was only able to capture the perceptions of those respondents who knew Megafon' and that many see the videos without knowing Megafon is behind them - so the 34% is neither a population exposure rate nor an upper bound; (c) the Figure 1 slices (17%, 10%, 23%, 32%, 11%, 7%) as transcribed do not reconcile with the 34% stated in the text, so even the composition of 'at least once a week' cannot be verified from this file. If the review does count self-reported encounter with a state-propaganda source as source-level RECALL, this paper would flip to INCLUDE on that single number, with denominator n = 480 aware respondents.

Other numbers deliberately not extracted: (1) '54% of all political advertising featured hostile narratives' and 'The ruling party and its satellite organization were responsible for 98% of the total EUR 2.5 million spent on promoting such narratives' - both attributed to Political Capital et al. (2024), i.e. cited from elsewhere (R8), and 'hostile narratives' is a rhetoric category, not a falsity judgement. (2) Topical counts within the 105 videos: 39 on Peter Magyar, 22 on the Ukraine war, 10 on the 'dollar left/dollar media' - topics, not veracity. (3) Poll shares that are not misinformation exposure: 43% knew at least one influencer, 30% name recognition for the most prominent influencer, 20% recognised the name Megafon, 76% of those who recognised the name knew Megafon has close ties to the government, 2% thought it closer to the opposition, 11% thought it independent, 30% knew Megafon publishes paid content, 64% said its content is not credible (Figure 3, n = 204), 39% never finish watching (Figure 2, n = 129), 37% irritated a lot / 34% slightly. (4) Focus-group material (26 participants) is qualitative. (5) Figures cited from other literature (e.g. 65% of foreign influence efforts linked to Russia; 19% of Republicans and 10% of Democrats endorsing political violence; a 39% reduction in intergroup empathy) are from other studies and unrelated to prevalence of misinformation exposure.

rob.design: Mixed-methods case study of the Megafon influencer network during the 2024 European Parliament and Hungarian municipal campaigns, conducted within the Hungarian Digital Media Observatory. (1) Qualitative content analysis of the 105 Megafon videos with the highest advertising spend between 1 February and 9 June 2024, selected from the Facebook Ad Library (at least HUF 204.8 million, ca. EUR 500,000, of advertising; Meta publishes only banded figures, so spend was computed at the minimum threshold). No coding scheme, coder count, coding categories or inter-coder reliability are reported, and no video is scored for truth or falsity. (2) Four online focus groups, 26 participants (14 pro-government, 12 opposition; balanced by gender, varied by education, occupation and residence), recruited by the Median Institute, held in early May 2024, with three Megafon videos screened. (3) Public opinion poll of 1,000 respondents representative of the Hungarian adult population by gender, age, education and municipality type, fielded 13-24 May 2024, margin of error +/-3.2 percentage points; no response rate reported. Several poll items are asked only of filtered subsamples (n = 480 aware of Megafon or an influencer; n = 204 who knew the name Megafon; n = 129 who had seen an influencer), which the authors acknowledge excludes the least-aware and most vulnerable users.
rob.item6_quote: Hostile narratives are necessarily based on the use of untrue or distorted facts. [...] This narration constructs a story that exaggerates, distorts, or reframes specific characteristics of the person or group designated as the enemy. In all cases, the story as a whole gives a false picture of the person or group concerned.
rob.item10_quote: A third of the respondents (34%) who had heard of one of the influencers or the name Megafon came across videos associated with the group at least once a week. [Figure 1 note: A share of respondents who knew at least one of the Megafon influencers or Megafon itself (n = 480).] - quoted as the closest numerator/denominator sentence in the paper; it is an encounter-frequency item about a named influencer group, not a share of content or respondents classified as misinformation.
